objective: Determining whether available data meets solution needs, and conveying data readiness to leadership in business-relevant terms
secondaryObjectives: Defining required data: types, formats, volume, and quality standards mapped to business objectives

sources.cite: PMI Certified Professional in Managing AI (PMI-CPMAI) Examination Content Outline (September 2025): Responsible and Trustworthy AI 15%, Business Needs and Solutions 26%, Data Needs 26%, Model Development and Evaluation 16%, Operationalize 17%
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch of a training provider's syllabus page that restates the outline in its own words (PMI's PDF did not come up in search). Restated: data evaluation (assess data quality; analyze distributions for bias or gaps; exploratory data analysis); model governance (lifecycle management, versioning and change control, monitor performance and detect drift). The objective wording here is the course seed's; PMI's own wording is to verify. Reused for REQ-336 from this course's loan-data-bias-pmicpmai (the same reading and date); the objective wording is the course seed's.

The organization, the data, the figures and the people are fictional. The minutes or days each step takes and the effects of each decision are teaching simplifications for exam practice, not measured values.

brief.situation: You manage an AI project at Larkfield Outfitters, a fictional retailer, to forecast product returns so warehouses can staff for them. Leadership wants a go or no-go on building the model next month.
handover: The business objective: forecast weekly returns per warehouse within 10%.
Two years of order and return data exist across three systems.
howItWorks: The console shows the open dataset, its quality flags and a table of the checks and their results.
Move on a step at a time. A decision comes to you at each step; before the first, you can read the evidence.
At the end you write the record and a short reflection.

then.log: Step 2: the pilot forecasts store returns 35% too low; one warehouse is short-staffed through a sale.
Step 3: the purchased data trains a model that misreads Larkfield's seasonal peaks; the sponsor questions the spend.
Step 4: store warehouses staff to the model; Black Friday returns overwhelm two of them.

fitPrompt.title: Does the data meet the need?
fitPrompt.context: Store returns lack reasons and order links.

choices.label: Map required data to the forecast objective: store returns need order links and at least one more seasonal cycle; mark the store forecast not ready and the online forecast ready

effects.log: The gap is documented by requirement.

choices.feedback: Data readiness is judged by whether the data meets the solution's needs, mapped to the business objective.

choices.label: Call it ready: two years and millions of rows
choices.feedback: Volume hides the missing store links and short history.

choices.label: Fill missing store return reasons with the online reasons' distribution
choices.feedback: The model would learn online customers' behavior and apply it to stores.

planPrompt.title: What to do about stores
planPrompt.context: Stores could start capturing order links and reasons.

choices.label: Start with online returns now; have stores capture order links and reasons from next month, and revisit stores after one more peak season
choices.feedback: When data is not ready for part of the solution, phase the scope and fix data capture at the source.

choices.label: Pause the whole project until store data is complete
choices.feedback: The online forecast, which is ready, also waits a year.

choices.label: Buy a third-party returns dataset for other retailers' stores
choices.feedback: Another retailer's stores do not describe Larkfield's customers.

choices.label: Report: go for online warehouses now (60% of volume, within the 10% target in testing); stores not ready until order links and one more peak season exist; what that means for staffing
choices.feedback: Leaders need readiness expressed as what can be forecast, how well and when, not as data-quality jargon.

choices.label: Send the data-quality profile report
choices.feedback: Accurate but leaves leadership to interpret null rates.

choices.label: Report 'data ready, go' for everything
choices.feedback: Leadership commits store staffing to a forecast the data cannot support.

reflection.question: Write the data readiness record for leadership.

parts.label: Readiness
parts.criteria: Online ready; stores not ready (no order links, 9 months of history).
parts.modelAnswer: Online returns data meets the forecast's needs; store returns lack order links and a second peak season.

parts.label: Decision
parts.criteria: Go for online now; stores capture links from next month.
parts.modelAnswer: We start with online warehouses (60% of volume) now; stores begin capturing order links and reasons next month and will be reassessed after the next peak.

scoring.modelReasoning: Data readiness is judged against what the solution needs, mapped to the business objective, not by data volume. Where data falls short, phase the scope and fix capture at the source rather than inventing labels. Report readiness to leaders in business terms: what can be predicted, how well and when.
